links.targetTitle: Osero's Pioneer Incentive Pool is not a segregated account —
Spark nets its Upkeep Rebate against the fees it owes rather

title: The rebate can exceed fees owed, and the excess is distributed to token holders as a surplus
content:
Two adjacent steps in the Upkeep Rebate Routine Protocol define where the money goes. A.6.1.1.7.2.3.2.2.1.2.1.2: "When paying Ecosystem Upkeep fees, Osero deducts the rebate from the fees it pays." A.6.1.1.7.2.3.2.2.1.2.1.3 then refers to Operational GovOps reviewing the calculation "before executing a return of surplus to token holders."

The existence of a surplus step tells us the rebate is not capped at the fee. An Agent holding enough peer-Agent tokens can generate a rebate larger than its own upkeep obligation, and the excess does not stay with the Agent — it flows through to OSERO token holders.

That completes the incentive chain from the previous claim. Cross-holding does not merely reduce an Agent's costs to zero; past that point it becomes a distribution to the Agent's own holders. The rebate is therefore a yield source, not just a discount, and the marginal incentive to hold peer tokens does not switch off when fees are covered.

It also explains why the verification step is placed where it is. A pure fee deduction would be checked by whoever collects the fee; a payout to token holders needs an independent check before funds leave, which is exactly the blocking review the next section assigns to Operational GovOps.
description: Netting against upkeep fees is the first claim on the rebate; A.6.1.1.7.2.3.2.2.1.2.1.3 shows anything left over becomes a return to OSERO holders, subject to review.
